title: Image to Base64 Converter: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Image to Base64 Converter: Turn an image into a Base64 data URI — for embedding in HTML and CSS. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it, a worked example…
content: The [Image to Base64 Converter](/image-to-base64-converter) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Turn an image into a Base64 data URI — for embedding in HTML and CSS. Enter your image file and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like. Turn an image into a Base64 data URI — a long text string you can paste straight into HTML or CSS to embed the image without a separate file. Pick an image (up to 5 MB), and the tool reads it with the browser's FileReader and shows the data URI, its size, and a copy button. The file never leaves your browser: nothing is uploaded. Base64 makes the file about a third larger, so it suits small images — icons, logos and tiny illustrations — not photographs. ## How to use the Image to Base64 Converter Start by typing or pasting your image file. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. The steps below walk through each input in order. 1. Choose an image file (PNG, JPG, GIF, SVG, WebP — up to 5 MB). 2. Read the data URI and its size. 3. Copy it and paste it into your HTML or CSS. ## How it works The [Image to Base64 Converter](/image-to-base64-converter) works straight from the values you enter: change an input and the result updates immediately, with no page reload and no waiting. Everything happens in your browser, so your entries never leave your device. Try it with a few different values and you will quickly get a feel for how the inputs move the result. ## Worked example Here is a typical example. A 2 KB PNG logo becomes a data URI starting “data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo…” — about 2.7 KB of text, which you can paste into an or a CSS background. Try the same figures in the [Image to Base64 Converter](/image-to-base64-converter) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves. ## Trying it out The fastest way to see what the [Image to Base64 Converter](/image-to-base64-converter) does is to open it and enter values you already know the answer for. Change one input at a time and watch how the result responds — that tells you more than any description. Everything runs in your browser, so you can experiment freely: nothing is saved, sent or tracked. ## What a data URI is A data URI packs a whole file into a URL: data:image/png;base64, followed by the file's bytes encoded as text. The browser decodes it and shows the image, with no separate request. It is handy for tiny images that would cost more as a separate download than as text — a logo in an email signature, an icon in a single-file page, or a background in a stylesheet. ## Why not to Base64 everything Base64 encoding makes a file about 37% larger, and the browser cannot cache it separately from the page — every page load re-downloads the image inside the HTML. For anything bigger than a few kilobytes, a normal image file is faster. As a rule of thumb: icons and small logos, yes; photographs, no. ## Tips A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself: - Best for small images — icons and logos under a few kilobytes. - The output is about a third larger than the original file. - Use the CSS or HTML format button to get a ready-to-paste snippet. ## Frequently asked questions ### What is a Base64 data URI? A way to embed a whole image in a text string: data:image/png;base64, followed by the image bytes encoded as text. Paste it into an tag or CSS and the browser shows the image with no separate file. You can use it as often as you like, and because nothing is uploaded, stored or tracked, there is nothing to delete afterwards. ### Is my image uploaded anywhere? No. The file is read by your browser's FileReader and never leaves your device. Try it with your own numbers in the [Image to Base64 Converter](/image-to-base64-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds. ### Why is the output larger than the image? Base64 uses four text characters for every three bytes, so the output is about 37% larger than the original file. Try it with your own numbers in the [Image to Base64 Converter](/image-to-base64-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds. ### When should I use a data URI? For small images — icons, logos, tiny illustrations. For photographs or anything large, a normal image file is faster because the browser can cache it separately. You can use it as often as you like, and because nothing is uploaded, stored or tracked, there is nothing to delete afterwards. ## Related tools The [URL Encoder](/url-encoder), [URL Decoder](/url-decoder), [Base64 Encoder](/base64-encoder) and [Base64 Decoder](/base64-decoder) cover related calculations in the same category.
